It just seems to me that this civilian posturing is ironic, though the gun toting folks whom showed up to "protect" soldiers won't see it that way.

The irony lost on those that pick up arms for the fallen is this: they are subscribing to the same mantra as their enemy. My fellow countrymen have been killed, so I must arm myself.

Poignant, yet quickly forgotten was the response in Norway to the island shooting tragedy. The same response was given in the recent racially motivated killings at that church. "We forgive you." It's crazy how disarming it is to your enemy when you stop fighting back. Sure, there is an initial period where the enemy will continue to push, but then there is no struggle, and so the enemy stops fighting.

From the article:

Lifetime use among seventh to ninth graders fell from 14.01% to 10.6%. Lifetime heroin use among 16-18 year olds fell from 2.5% to 1.8%.

Yes. I read the article. So far as I can tell there's no justification for substituting "crack" for "heroin" in the article and assuming the results will be the same. If you can provide any justification for this rationale I will welcome it.

Please note question above does not ask what would happen if heroin were legal. Please refrain from conflating crack and heroin for the purpose of this discussion.
Crack and heroin both lead to adverse health effects, chronic illness, higher risk for std's, and addiction. I see no reason why the two cannot be interchangable in this conversation.

There's a key distinction that the article fails to point out however. In reality Portugal hasn't "legalized" drugs. They've decriminalized possession for personal use. There's a HUGE difference between that and full on legalization ala alcohol and tobacco. Under Portugese laws, if you posess more than a ten day supply of a particular substance it qualifies as posession to distribute, which is still a crime.
